feature_intro.name: feature_intro
feature_intro.label: Overview
feature_intro.title: What Is a Literature Review Generator?
feature_intro.description:
A literature review is a critical synthesis of what has already been published on a topic: its purpose is to show what is known, where studies agree or clash, and where the gaps remain. A literature review generator is an AI drafting aid for exactly that chapter. You give it a research topic, your assignment constraints, and optionally the sources and notes you have already collected; it drafts the structure and prose of a narrative literature review — introduction, theme-based synthesis, tensions and gaps, and a conclusion — plus an 'Evidence to Verify' checklist of every claim that still needs a real source.

It is deliberately not a research database, citation manager, or systematic-review tool. It does not search Google Scholar or any publisher database, and it never invents bibliographic details. The draft is a starting point you verify, revise, and cite against your own reading — which is exactly how a defensible literature review gets written.

example_section.name: example_outline
example_section.label: EXAMPLE
example_section.title: Literature Review Outline Example
example_section.description: Every draft follows this shape — a standard narrative review template you can build on once each claim is sourced. Yours is generated from your topic and constraints, with [source needed] markers wherever evidence still belongs.

items.title: ## Introduction
items.description: Scope of the review, how the field is organised, and how the themes were chosen.
items.content: “Research on formative assessment has grown rapidly over the past two decades, yet findings remain uneven across secondary science contexts. [source needed]”

items.title: ### Theme: Feedback and motivation
items.description: The body synthesises perspectives theme by theme instead of summarising paper by paper.
items.content: “Several strands of work converge on the claim that timely, specific feedback predicts engagement, while award-based incentives show mixed results. [source needed]”

items.title: ## Tensions and Gaps
items.description: Where studies disagree, which questions stay open, and what remains under-researched.
items.content: “Findings conflict on whether extrinsic rewards crowd out intrinsic motivation in adolescent samples. [source needed]”

items.title: ## Conclusion
items.description: What the balance of the reviewed context suggests and what a reader should take away.
items.content: “Taken together, the literature points to feedback quality — not volume — as the lever most worth further study. [source needed]”

items.title: ## Evidence to Verify
items.description: A checklist of every claim that still needs a real source — never a fabricated reference list.
items.content: “☐ ‘Feedback quality predicts engagement’ — search: formative feedback + student motivation + secondary school”

source_responsibility.name: source_responsibility
source_responsibility.label: Sources
source_responsibility.title: How the Generator Handles Sources
source_responsibility.description: Clear boundaries, so nothing in your draft pretends to be sourced.

items.title: No invented references
items.description: The generator never fabricates citations, author-year references, DOIs, page numbers, quotes, or specific study findings. If a claim has no source behind it, the draft says so with a [source needed] marker instead.

items.title: Your notes as context
items.description: Anything you paste — reading notes, themes, half-kept references — is treated strictly as user-provided context. The draft refers to those works only with the details you gave, and marks anything incomplete for verification.

items.title: A checklist, not a bibliography
items.description: Every claim that still needs evidence is collected in the 'Evidence to Verify' section, phrased so you can search for it. Placeholders stay visible and separate; they never masquerade as a reference list.

faq_section.title: Literature Review Generator FAQs
faq_section.description: The academic-integrity questions students ask most.

items.title: Is this a citation generator?
items.description: No. The generator drafts the structure and prose of a narrative literature review. It does not retrieve, format, or verify citations, and it never invents bibliographic details. You add real references from sources you have actually read.

items.title: Does it search Google Scholar or academic databases?
items.description: No. It only works with the topic, constraints, and sources you provide. It cannot prove coverage of a field, and it does not claim to. Searching the literature remains your job — the draft tells you exactly what to search for.

items.title: Can I submit the generated review directly?
items.description: No. The output is a drafting aid. You must read it critically, verify every claim against real sources, add genuine citations, revise the prose, and comply with your institution's policy on AI-assisted work before submitting anything.

items.title: What happens if I don't paste any sources?
items.description: The draft is written without naming specific studies, and every claim that needs evidence is listed in the 'Evidence to Verify' checklist instead of a fake reference list. Paste your notes on a second pass to tighten the synthesis.

items.title: Is this a systematic review tool?
items.description: No. It drafts narrative literature reviews only. It does not support PRISMA screening, protocol registration, or completeness claims, and it will not pretend your review was systematic.

items.title: Is the Literature Review Generator free?
items.description: Yes. Anonymous visitors can generate drafts with the standard model for free. The Creative model follows the site-wide three-trial daily quota with sign-in, and Turnstile verification protects the endpoint from abuse.

items.title: How long should a literature review be?
items.description: It depends on your level and brief. As commonly cited guidance, undergraduate reviews often run 1,000–2,000 words and master's reviews 3,000–5,000, but your assignment brief always wins. The generator drafts at roughly 800, 1,500, or 2,500 words so you have a proportionate starting structure to expand with sourced material.

items.title: How many sources should be in a literature review?
items.description: There is no fixed number — it depends on the scope of your topic and your level. Commonly cited guidance is around 15–30 sources for an undergraduate review and 40 or more for a master's review, but breadth matters more than count. Because the generator never invents sources, its 'Evidence to Verify' checklist tells you exactly which claims need one.

items.title: Does the generator follow APA format?
items.description: The generator drafts structure and prose, not citations — so it does not format references in APA, MLA, Harvard, or any other style. You add and format real references in the style your department requires. Tip: paste your required referencing style, abstract, and section headings into the assignment brief so the draft respects them from the start.
